seo.title: Ignatius of Antioch: the bishop who begged Rome not to save him
seo.description: Ignatius of Antioch in plain words: seven letters written in chains on the road to the lions, his real words, his feast days, and the legends.

who: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch in Syria in the early 100s. Condemned to the wild beasts, he was taken under guard to Rome. On the way he wrote seven letters, to six churches and to Polycarp. He begged the Christians of Rome not to save him. He died in Rome, most likely about 110.

roles.line: Seven letters, from Smyrna and Troas

All that survives of his writing

tidbits.text: His “ten leopards” is the oldest use of the word leopard in any writing that survives, notes Arthur McGiffert, the translator of Eusebius.

cite.text: McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36

tidbits.text: He may have coined the Greek word for “Christianity”, says the scholar Maia Kotrosits. He sets it beside the word for “Judaism” in his letters to the Magnesians and the Philadelphians.

cite.text: Maia Kotrosits, in Philip A. Harland, Ethnic Relations and Migration in the Ancient World

tidbits.text: For centuries the Syriac Orthodox patriarchs of Antioch, once called Jacobites, have taken the name Ignatius when they come to office, noted Lightfoot in 1889.

cite.text: Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

tidbits.text: In Lotto's painting at the top of this page, he offers the Christ Child his heart, marked with Christ's monogram. The Borghese inventory of 1693 took the heart for a loaf of bread.

cite.text: Galleria Borghese, catalogue entry for Lotto's Madonna and Child with Saints Ignatius of Antioch and Onuphrius

facts.label: Born
facts.text: Nothing is known of his birth or family. Lightfoot thought he was raised a pagan and came to Christ as a grown man.

facts.label: Bishop of
facts.text: **Antioch in Syria**, today **Antakya in Turkey**. Its second bishop, after Evodius, by Eusebius's count, or the third counting Peter.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: At **Rome**, thrown to the wild beasts, under the emperor **Trajan**. Eusebius's *Chronicle* says 107. Lightfoot put it “within a few years of A.D. 110, before or after”.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: Jerome says his remains lay at **Antioch**, in the cemetery outside the gate to Daphne. The *Roman Martyrology* says they were later brought to the church of **St Clement** in Rome.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Theophorus**, “the God-bearer”: a second name, as Saul was also called Paul. **Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer**, in the Orthodox churches. An **Apostolic Father**, one of the first Christian writers after the apostles.

facts.label: His name
facts.text: Latin. Severus, a patriarch of Antioch in the 500s, linked it to {la|ignis}, fire, for the love that burned in him. Lightfoot called that derivation “altogether false”.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox, Copts and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A bishop, often between two lions. In the West he may hold a heart marked with the name of Jesus, from a medieval legend.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Seven letters: to the churches of **Ephesus**, **Magnesia**, **Tralles**, **Rome**, **Philadelphia** and **Smyrna**, and to **Polycarp**.

portrait.alt: A Byzantine mosaic of glittering gold and silver-white stones: the head of Saint Ignatius, an old bishop with a high bald forehead, wide dark eyes and a long pointed beard, above a white stole marked with black crosses

west.text: His day in Rome from the 1100s until 1969, and in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**.
**Catholic** memorial. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.
The bringing of his relics to Antioch, in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**.

east.text: The **Coptic** Church, on 24 Kiahk in its own calendar, for his martyrdom. Churches on the old calendar keep 20 December on this day too.
The bringing of his relics to Antioch, in the **Orthodox** calendar, as the **OCA** keeps it.
The **Coptic** Church again, on 7 Epip, for his death in Rome.
His chief day in the **Orthodox** churches, as in the **OCA**. The **Greeks** kept it “to this day”, noted the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* in 1885.

feasts.note: Why so many days? The oldest is 17 October. A Syriac calendar of the late 300s already has him there. Rome kept him on 1 February from the 1100s, and in 1969 moved him back to his old Syrian day. The later *Martyrdom of Ignatius* says he died on 20 December. Lightfoot thought 20 December was really the day his relics were laid in Antioch's old Temple of Fortune, in the 400s. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later: 20 December falls on 2 January, and 29 January on 11 February.

traits.title: on fire to die for Christ
traits.text: He asked Rome not to rescue him, and he meant it. The beasts in the arena had been known to shy away from some prisoners. If they shied from him, he would make them come: “But if they be unwilling to assail me, I will compel them to do so. Pardon me [in this]: I know what is for my benefit.” And then: “Now I begin to be a disciple.”

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 5

traits.title: wary of praise
traits.text: He feared his own pride. “I have great knowledge in God, but I restrain myself, lest, I should perish through boasting.” Kind words hurt him: “For they that speak to me [in the way of commendation] scourge me.”

cite.text: Letter to the Trallians, chapter 4

traits.title: sure he was the least
traits.text: He called himself a condemned man, never an apostle. Of the church in Syria he wrote, “I am ashamed to be counted one of them; for indeed I am not worthy, as being the very last of them, and one born out of due time.” Lightfoot read such lines as the words of a late convert, troubled by his past. He was one of those “broken” natures, Lightfoot wrote, out of which “God's heroes are made”.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 9; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

traits.title: loud for unity
traits.text: At Philadelphia he cried out in church: “I cried, I spoke with a loud voice: Give heed to the bishop, and to the presbytery and deacons.” Some thought someone had told him of a split there. No one had, he said: the Spirit had. He called himself “a man devoted to unity”.

cite.text: Letter to the Philadelphians, chapters 7 and 8

traits.title: gentle in deed, fierce in word
traits.text: He told the Ephesians to meet hatred with kindness: “Be ye meek in response to their wrath, humble in opposition to their boasting: to their blasphemies return your prayers”. Yet he called false teachers “ravening dogs, who bite secretly” and “beasts in the shape of men”. Even so, he asked the church to pray for them, “if by any means they may be brought to repentance”.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapters 7 and 10; Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 4

traits.title: a pastor's eye
traits.text: His advice to Polycarp is plain and practical. “Every kind of wound is not healed with the same plaster.” Anyone can love the easy ones: “seek by meekness to subdue the more troublesome.” And: “Let not widows be neglected.”

cite.text: Letter to Polycarp, chapters 2 and 4

traits.title: warm to his friends
traits.text: He names his friends one by one. At Smyrna he greets “Alce, my well-beloved, and the incomparable Daphnus”. To Rome he sends word of Crocus, “one dearly beloved by me”. Of Burrhus, the deacon who travelled with him, he wrote: “And I would that all may imitate him, as being a pattern of a minister of God.”

cite.text: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapters 12 and 13; Letter to the Romans, chapter 10

said.lede: We have the letter of a friend who met him in chains, a line quoted two generations later, and a sermon preached in his own city. Later readers still argue over him.

quotes.q: …by them ye may be greatly profited; for they treat of faith and patience, and all things that tend to edification in our Lord.
quotes.who: Polycarp of Smyrna, sending copies of his letters to Philippi

cite.text: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 13

quotes.q: As a certain man of ours said, when he was condemned to the wild beasts because of his testimony with respect to God: “I am the wheat of Christ, and am ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of God.”
quotes.who: Irenaeus of Lyons, about 180. He does not give his name.

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 5, chapter 28

quotes.q: …Ignatius, who was chosen bishop of Antioch, second in succession to Peter, and whose fame is still celebrated by a great many.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36

quotes.q: Ye sent forth a Bishop, and received a martyr; ye sent him forth with prayers, and ye received him with crowns.
quotes.who: John Chrysostom, then a priest of Antioch, preaching to its people on his feast

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homily on Saint Ignatius, chapter 5

quotes.q: In him, indeed, the lions encountered a lion, one truly begotten of “the Lion of the tribe of Judah.”
quotes.who: A. Cleveland Coxe, American editor of the *Ante-Nicene Fathers*, 1885

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note to the Epistles of Ignatius

quotes.q: …the whole system of Catholic doctrine may be discovered, at least in outline, not to say in parts filled up, in the course of his seven epistles.
quotes.who: John Henry Newman, as quoted in the *Catholic Encyclopedia*

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), “St. Ignatius of Antioch”

quotes.q: He is the incarnation, as it were, of the three closely connected ideas: the glory of martyrdom, the omnipotence of episcopacy, and the hatred of heresy and schism.
quotes.who: Philip Schaff, a Protestant church historian, quoted by McGiffert, 1890

cite.text: McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36

moments.title: Bishop of a great city
moments.text: Antioch was one of the great cities of the empire, and its church was old. It was there that the disciples were first called Christians. Ignatius was its second bishop, after Evodius, says Eusebius. Chrysostom said “the hands of the blessed apostles touched his sacred head”. Theodoret said Peter ordained him. Lightfoot called such stories “excrescences on the earliest tradition”, which calls him only an apostolic man.

cite.text: Acts 11:26; Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 22; John Chrysostom, Homily on Saint Ignatius; Theodoret, Letter 151; Lightfoot (1889)

moments.title: Condemned
moments.text: Of his arrest and trial we know nothing, beyond his letters. The church at Antioch was in trouble. He was sentenced to the beasts, and sent to Rome to die in the arena. Again and again he calls himself “a condemned man”. He did not appeal, and did not want to. As Lightfoot put it, “He goes to Rome therefore for the execution of his sentence.”

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 12; Letter to the Romans, chapter 4; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

moments.title: Ten leopards
moments.text: He travelled chained to a guard of ten soldiers. The road itself was a fight: “From Syria even unto Rome I fight with beasts, both by land and sea, both by night and day, being bound to ten leopards, I mean a band of soldiers, who, even when they receive benefits, show themselves all the worse.” The gifts his friends gave them, Lightfoot thought, only made them greedier.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 5; Lightfoot (1889)

moments.title: “That remains to be proved”
moments.text: At Philadelphia, in Asia, he met a divided church. Some said, “If I do not find it in the ancient Scriptures, I will not believe the Gospel.” When he answered, “It is written”, they said, “That remains to be proved.” His reply: “But to me Jesus Christ is in the place of all that is ancient: His cross, and death, and resurrection, and the faith which is by Him, are undefiled monuments of antiquity”.

cite.text: Letter to the Philadelphians, chapter 8

moments.title: A guest of Polycarp
moments.text: At Smyrna he stayed with Polycarp, its bishop. Word had gone ahead down the southern road, and three churches sent men to meet him. From Ephesus came its bishop Onesimus, “a man of inexpressible love”, with the deacon Burrhus, Crocus, Euplus and Fronto. From Magnesia came its young bishop Damas, two presbyters and a deacon. From Tralles came its bishop Polybius. In them, he wrote, he saw their whole churches. He wrote four letters from Smyrna.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapters 1 and 2; Letter to the Magnesians, chapter 2; Letter to the Trallians, chapter 1; Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36; Lightfoot (1889)

moments.title: Do not save me
moments.text: One letter went ahead of him to Rome. The Christians there had friends of influence, who might win him a pardon. He begged them not to try: “For I am afraid of your love, lest it should do me an injury.” And: “Suffer me to become food for the wild beasts, through whose instrumentality it will be granted me to attain to God.” Then comes his most famous line, about the wheat of God.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapters 1 and 4

moments.title: Good news from home
moments.text: At Troas he heard that the church at Antioch was at peace. He wrote three more letters, to Philadelphia, to Smyrna and to Polycarp. He asked each church to send a messenger to Antioch to share its joy. Then the guards set sail with no warning: “I have not been able to write to all the Churches, because I must suddenly sail from Troas to Neapolis”. He asked Polycarp to write to the rest for him.

cite.text: Letter to the Philadelphians, chapter 10; Letter to Polycarp, chapters 7 and 8

moments.title: The curtain drops
moments.text: From Neapolis the prisoners went on to Philippi. The church there welcomed them and walked with them, “those who were bound in chains, the fitting ornaments of saints”, Polycarp wrote. The Philippians then asked Polycarp for copies of Ignatius's letters, and any news of him. Polycarp had none to give. “Here the curtain drops on the career of the martyr,” wrote Lightfoot.

cite.text: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapters 1, 9 and 13; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

words.note: Seven letters survive, all written in a few weeks on the road. This page quotes them only in their shorter Greek form, the one scholars call the middle recension, in the English of Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, printed in the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* of 1885. Why that matters is told below.

feature.q: I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.
feature.ctx: Written from Smyrna, weeks before he reached Rome. It is the first line of his that anyone is known to have quoted: Irenaeus used it about 180, without giving his name.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 4

quotes.q: It is better for a man to be silent and be [a Christian], than to talk and not to be one. It is good to teach, if he who speaks also acts.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 15

quotes.q: For the beginning is faith, and the end is love.
quotes.who: On the two things that begin and end a Christian life.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 14

quotes.q: My love has been crucified, and there is no fire in me desiring to be fed; but there is within me a water that liveth and speaketh, saying to me inwardly, Come to the Father.
quotes.who: Origen, a century later, read “my love” here as Christ Himself.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 7; Origen, Commentary on the Song of Songs, prologue, as given by Lightfoot (1889)

quotes.q: …breaking one and the same bread, which is the medicine of immortality, and the antidote to prevent us from dying, but [which causes] that we should live for ever in Jesus Christ.
quotes.who: On the Eucharist, the bread broken together in one church.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 20

quotes.q: They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again.
quotes.who: Of teachers who said Christ only seemed to have a body.

cite.text: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 7

quotes.q: He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate; He was truly crucified, and [truly] died, in the sight of beings in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth.
quotes.who: Against the same teachers. His word “truly” answers their “seemed”.

cite.text: Letter to the Trallians, chapter 9

quotes.q: There is one Physician Who is possessed both of flesh and spirit; both made and not made; God existing in flesh; true life in death; both of Mary and of God; first possible and then impossible, even Jesus Christ our Lord.
quotes.who: On who Christ is. “Possible” here means able to suffer.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 7

quotes.q: Look for Him Who is above all time, eternal and invisible, yet Who became visible for our sakes.

cite.text: Letter to Polycarp, chapter 3

quotes.q: A Christian has not power over himself, but must always be ready for the service of God.
quotes.who: To Polycarp, asking him to send a messenger to Antioch.

cite.text: Letter to Polycarp, chapter 7

quotes.q: Nothing is more precious than peace, by which all war, both in heaven and earth, is brought to an end.
quotes.who: To the Ephesians, urging them to meet often.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 13

extras.title: Which letters are his?
extras.lede: Fifteen letters carry his name. Which ones are really his has been argued over for four hundred years. Here is where it stands, in the words of both sides.

items.title: Eight forgeries
items.text: Three letters exist only in Latin: two to the apostle John and one to the Virgin Mary. Five more are in Greek: to Tarsus, to Antioch, to Hero, to Philippi and to Mary of Cassobola. Neither Eusebius nor Jerome mentions them. No one defends them now.
items.quote: It is now the universal opinion of critics, that the first eight of these professedly Ignatian letters are spurious.

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note to the Epistles of Ignatius

items.title: The long version
items.text: The seven real letters also survive in a padded form, with lines added and six forged letters bound in. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* dates it to about 400, the work of one writer who padded them “to lend weight to the personal views of its author”. Until 1644 this was the form most readers knew. John Calvin, writing before then, called the letters under his name “absurdities”: “Nothing can be more nauseating, than the absurdities which have been published under the name of Ignatius”. Then Archbishop James Ussher found an old Latin copy of the shorter text.
items.quote: Ussher had rediscovered the middle recension.

cite.text: William R. Schoedel, Anchor Bible Dictionary (1992), as given by Early Christian Writings; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Calvin, Institutes, Book 1, chapter 13

items.title: Only three?
items.text: In the 1840s William Cureton found three of the letters in Syriac, shorter still: to Polycarp, to the Ephesians and to the Romans. He was sure these three alone were real, and hoped the world would soon agree. Lightfoot and the German scholar Theodor Zahn answered him at length. In McGiffert's words, their defence of the seven may be “regarded as finally settling the matter”. Schoedel calls the Syriac “merely an abridgment of a Syriac version of the middle recension”.
items.quote: …the only true and genuine letters of the venerable Bishop of Antioch that have either come down to our times, or were ever known in the earliest ages of the Christian Church.

cite.text: William Cureton (1849), as quoted in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36; Schoedel (1992)

items.title: Are even the seven his?
items.text: A minority of scholars doubt it. McGiffert, who did not share their doubts, named the two main reasons in 1890: “the highly developed form of church government which they reveal; and secondly, the attacks upon heresy contained in them.” Both looked too late for Trajan's day. Robert Joly argued the case in 1979. Others move Ignatius himself later: Timothy Barnes argued in 2008 that “the letters were probably written in the 140s”. Most still side with the old defenders. In Schoedel's words, “the researches of Zahn (1873) and Lightfoot (1885, 1889) and their followers continue to dominate the scholarship.”
items.quote: I must own I have found it a very difficult question.

cite.text: Nathaniel Lardner (1743), as quoted in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1; McGiffert (1890); Schoedel (1992); Timothy D. Barnes, “The Date of Ignatius”, Expository Times (2008)

extras.title: Hard questions
extras.lede: Three things in his letters divide or trouble readers. Here they are, in the words of those who defend him and those who question.

items.title: “Do nothing without the bishop”
items.text: No early writer presses the bishop's place harder. “See that ye all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as ye would the apostles”. Catholic and Orthodox readers see here the Church's order from the start. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* found in him “the threefold character of the hierarchy” and even “the primacy of the See of Rome”. Lutherans of the Missouri Synod honour his stress on “the unity of the Church found in her bishops”. Protestant critics read him otherwise. Philip Schaff called him “the earliest advocate of the hierarchical principle in both its good and its evil points”. The American editor of the *Ante-Nicene Fathers*, A. Cleveland Coxe, found his letter to Rome “utterly inconsistent” with a bishop of Rome over his own.
items.quote: Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.

cite.text: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 8; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod, Commemorations; Schaff, quoted by McGiffert (1890); Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note

items.title: “It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize”
items.text: He wrote hard words about keeping the Jewish law. “For if we still live according to the Jewish law, we acknowledge that we have not received grace.” He praised those who lived “no longer observing the Sabbath, but living in the observance of the Lord's Day”. Some who pressed it on others were not Jews at all, as he says: “it is better to hearken to Christian doctrine from a man who has been circumcised, than to Judaism from one uncircumcised.” And he honoured the prophets: “let us also love the prophets”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* counts “the Judaizing heresies” among the errors he condemned. The scholar Maia Kotrosits reads his two words as linked, and not two rival religions. She warns that “These complex factors surrounding Ignatius' language later get erased”, as his words came to be read as Christianity replacing Judaism.
items.quote: It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize. For Christianity did not embrace Judaism, but Judaism Christianity, that so every tongue which believeth might be gathered together to God.

cite.text: Letter to the Magnesians, chapters 8 to 10; Letter to the Philadelphians, chapters 5 and 6; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Maia Kotrosits, in Philip A. Harland's Ethnic Relations and Migration in the Ancient World

items.title: Did he want to die?
items.text: His letter to Rome can shock. He will coax the beasts, and force them if they hang back. Critics call it a craving for death. Schaff wrote that his temper “carries him beyond the bounds of sobriety”. His defenders answer that the sentence was already passed. The American editor of the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* wrote that “he was already condemned, in law a dead man, and felt himself at liberty to glory in his tribulations.” Lightfoot went further: “It is a cheap wisdom which at the study table or over the pulpit desk declaims against the extravagance of the feelings and language of Ignatius, as the vision of martyrdom rose up before him.”
items.quote: Let fire and the cross; let the crowds of wild beasts; let tearings, breakings, and dislocations of bones; let cutting off of members; let shatterings of the whole body; and let all the dreadful torments of the devil come upon me: only let me attain to Jesus Christ.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 5; Schaff, quoted by McGiffert (1890); Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note; Lightfoot (1889)

myths.claim: “Where the bishop is present, there is the Catholic Church.”
myths.truth: A shortened line from quote sites. He wrote: “Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.” In Lightfoot's reading, “Jesus Christ is here said to stand to the universal Church, in the same relation as the bishop to the particular Church.”

cite.text: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 8; Lightfoot (1889); QuoteFancy

myths.claim: He was the child Jesus took in His arms and set among the disciples.
myths.truth: A late legend, built on his second name read as God-borne. It first appears at the end of the 800s, in Anastasius the Librarian, says Lightfoot. Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch, said the opposite: Ignatius was one “who had not even seen Him, nor enjoyed His companionship”. The Orthodox lives still tell it, as tradition.

cite.text: Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889); John Chrysostom, Homily on Saint Ignatius, chapter 4; OCA, 20 December

myths.claim: “My dear Jesus, my Savior, is so deeply written in my heart, that I feel confident, that if my heart were to be cut open and chopped to pieces, the name of Jesus would be found written on every piece.”
myths.truth: Not in his letters. It comes from a medieval legend that his heart, cut open, showed the name of Jesus in gold letters. Lightfoot found it in Vincent of Beauvais, in the 1200s, and said it “seems never to have gained any wide currency”. Quote sites give him the line anyway, and the Orthodox life tells the story as tradition.

cite.text: QuoteFancy; Lightfoot (1889); OCA, 20 December

myths.claim: He stood before the emperor Trajan at Antioch and called himself “He who has Christ within his breast”.
myths.truth: That scene comes from the *Martyrdom of Ignatius*, which claims to be by his friends. Lightfoot dated it to the 400s or 500s. He wrote that “the Martyrologies of Ignatius cannot be accepted as authentic history.” Its own translators noted that “no reference to this narrative is to be traced during the first six centuries”.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Ignatius, chapter 2; Lightfoot (1889); Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note to the Martyrdom

myths.claim: He was a disciple of the apostle John, with Polycarp.
myths.truth: Possible, but it comes late. The *Martyrdom of Ignatius* says so, and so do the Orthodox and Coptic lives. The earliest writers say only that he was the second bishop of Antioch. Lightfoot traced the link to John to later forms of Eusebius's *Chronicle*. He thought it could be true, but worthless as evidence.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Ignatius, chapter 3; Lightfoot (1889); OCA, 20 December; Coptic synaxarium, 24 Kiahk

myths.claim: He brought antiphonal singing into the Church, after a vision of angels.
myths.truth: The story is first told by the historian Socrates, about 440: Ignatius “saw a vision of angels hymning in alternate chants the Holy Trinity”. Lightfoot answered that “Antiphonal singing did not need to be suggested by a heavenly Vision.” The Greek chorus and the Jewish psalms had it already.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 8; Lightfoot, quoted in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, volume 3

myths.truth: Both are later dates. The 107 is from Eusebius's *Chronicle*. The 20 December is from the late *Martyrdom*. Lightfoot: “His martyrdom may with a high degree of probability be placed within a few years of A.D. 110, before or after.” He thought 20 December was the day his relics came to rest in Antioch's old Temple of Fortune.

cite.text: McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36; Martyrdom of Ignatius, chapter 7; Lightfoot (1889)

myths.claim: “Let no man's place, or dignity, or riches, puff him up; and let no man's low condition or poverty abase him.”
myths.truth: From the padded long version of his letter to the Smyrnaeans, not the real one. The real letter says less: “Let not [high] place puff any one up: for that which is worth all is faith and love, to which nothing is to be preferred.”

cite.text: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 6, in both versions; QuoteFancy

myths.claim: “If any one says that the Lord is a mere man, he is a Jew, a murderer of Christ.”
myths.truth: Not from the seven. It comes from a letter to Hero, a deacon of Antioch, forged in his name centuries later. So does the rule that anyone who fasts on the Lord's Day or the Sabbath “is a murderer of Christ”, from a forged letter to the Philippians. His real words on the Jewish law are under Hard questions.

cite.text: The spurious Letter to Hero, chapter 2, and Letter to the Philippians, chapter 13, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1

circle.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
circle.text: His host at Smyrna. Ignatius wrote him the only one of the seven letters addressed to a single person. Polycarp gathered the letters and sent them to Philippi.

cite.text: Letter to Polycarp; Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 13

circle.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
circle.text: Polycarp's pupil. About 180 he quoted the line about the wheat of God, the first writer known to quote Ignatius.

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 5, chapter 28; Lightfoot (1889)

circle.name: John Chrysostom
circle.text: As a priest of Antioch in the late 300s, he preached on the saint's feast, at the martyr's chapel outside the city.

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homily on Saint Ignatius; Lightfoot (1889)

circle.name: Peter
circle.text: Antioch counted him its first leader. Chrysostom said Ignatius took the office after him, and Theodoret that Peter ordained him. Ignatius wrote to Rome, “I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you.”

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homily on Saint Ignatius; Theodoret, Letter 151; Letter to the Romans, chapter 4

circle.name: Paul
circle.text: Like Paul, Ignatius went to Rome in chains. He called Paul the martyr “at whose feet may I be found, when I shall attain to God”.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 12

circle.name: Onesimus
circle.text: Bishop of Ephesus. He came to Smyrna to meet him, “a man of inexpressible love”.

cite.text: Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 1

circle.name: Burrhus
circle.text: A deacon of Ephesus. He stayed with Ignatius as far as Troas, and wrote at least two of his letters down for him.

cite.text: Letter to the Philadelphians, chapter 11; Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 12; Lightfoot (1889)

circle.name: Damas
circle.text: The young bishop of Magnesia. Ignatius told his church not to look down on him for his youth.

cite.text: Letter to the Magnesians, chapters 2 and 3

circle.name: Polybius
circle.text: Bishop of Tralles, who came to Smyrna to see him. In him, Ignatius wrote, “I beheld your whole multitude”.

cite.text: Letter to the Trallians, chapter 1

circle.name: Philo and Rheus Agathopus
circle.text: Two deacons, from Cilicia and from Syria, who followed him on the road as far as Troas and served him there.

cite.text: Letter to the Philadelphians, chapter 11; Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 10

circle.name: Alce
circle.text: A Christian woman of Smyrna he greeted in two letters. Half a century later, says Lightfoot, her brother Nicetes and her nephew Herod helped put Polycarp to death.

cite.text: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 13; Letter to Polycarp, chapter 8; Lightfoot (1889)

circle.name: Zosimus and Rufus
circle.text: Named by Polycarp beside “the blessed Ignatius”, perhaps prisoners on the same road. Nothing more is known of them.

cite.text: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 9; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36

circle.name: Evodius and Heros
circle.text: The bishops of Antioch before and after him, as Eusebius names them. Nothing else is known of either.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapters 22 and 36

death.big: He was thrown to the wild beasts at Rome, under the emperor Trajan, most likely within a few years of 110.
paras: No one who saw it wrote it down, as far as we know. Polycarp, writing soon after, asked the Philippians for news. Eusebius, about 300, had only this: “Report says that he was sent from Syria to Rome, and became food for wild beasts on account of his testimony to Christ.”

Chrysostom, preaching at Antioch in the late 300s, pictured it in the arena, “while the whole city was seated above him”. He told of the cities on the road carrying the martyr's remains home, “bearing him upon their shoulders as far as this city”.

By then his grave was shown outside Antioch, by the gate to Daphne. Jerome writes that “the remains of his body lie in Antioch outside the Daphnitic gate in the cemetery”. Lightfoot doubted they had ever left Rome. In the 400s the emperor Theodosius II had the relics carried into the city, to the old Temple of Fortune, which became the Church of Ignatius. Rome's martyrology says they were later brought back to Rome, to the church of St Clement.

later.title: The later story
later.text: The *Martyrdom of Ignatius* tells the rest, and claims to be by his friends on the road. In it he faces Trajan at Antioch and calls himself “He who has Christ within his breast”. He lands at Portus and is thrown to the beasts on 20 December, as the games close. Only “the harder portions of his holy remains” are left, and taken to Antioch. That night his friends see him in dreams. Lightfoot dated this account to the 400s or 500s.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Ignatius, chapters 2, 6 and 7; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

items.q: Rather entice the wild beasts, that they may become my tomb, and may leave nothing of my body; so that when I have fallen asleep [in death], I may be no trouble to any one.
It is good to set from the world unto God, that I may rise again to Him.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapters 2 and 4

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox, Copts and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: He was honoured early. By the late 300s Antioch kept his day, 17 October, and showed his grave outside the city. Chrysostom preached there on his feast.

When Rome cut back its calendar in 1969, it weighed the old martyrs honoured at Rome. Of most, little more than a name is known. Only four stayed as memorials that every church must keep: Agnes, Justin, Cornelius with Cyprian, and Ignatius. Rome also moved him from 1 February to 17 October, the day of the old Syrian calendar.
The later *Martyrdom* ends by asking its readers to keep his day:

quotes.q: …assembling ourselves together according to the time of his martyrdom, we may have fellowship with the champion and noble martyr of Christ, who trod under foot the devil, and perfected the course which, out of love to Christ, he had desired, in Christ Jesus our Lord.
quotes.who: The *Martyrdom of Ignatius*, a later account

cite.text: Martyrdom of Ignatius, chapter 7

prayer.title: From his letter to Rome
prayer.intro: In the middle of the letter he tells the Romans what he wants, and why.
prayer.q: All the pleasures of the world, and all the kingdoms of this earth, shall profit me nothing. It is better for me to die in behalf of Jesus Christ, than to reign over all the ends of the earth. “For what shall a man be profited, if he gain the whole world, but lose his own soul?” Him I seek, Who died for us: Him I desire, Who rose again for our sake. This is the gain which is laid up for me. Pardon me, brethren: do not hinder me from living, do not wish to keep me in a state of death; and while I desire to belong to God, do not ye give me over to the world. Suffer me to obtain pure light: when I have gone thither, I shall indeed be a man of God. Permit me to be an imitator of the passion of my God. If any one has Him within himself, let him consider what I desire, and let him have sympathy with me, as knowing how I am straitened.

cite.text: Letter to the Romans, chapter 6
